name: Blackout curtains

lead: Blackout curtains are heavy or foam- or film-backed window coverings that block most outside light from entering a bedroom. They are used to darken a room for sleep, particularly by shift workers, in cities with street lighting or in summer.

The looksmaxxing rationale is that sufficient, regular sleep supports skin, mood and hormone regulation, and that darkness aids sleep. Observational and small experimental studies link light during sleep with poorer sleep and metabolic effects, though no data were found for curtains specifically; the benefit is indirect.

paras: Blocking light avoids suppression of melatonin and reduces arousals from light exposure during sleep. A dark room helps maintain the circadian signal that it is night.

Curtains are low-risk. Gaps at the edges still let light leak, so fit matters. Total darkness can make waking harder in the morning, so some people pair them with a sunrise alarm or open them on waking. Claims that darkness alone repairs skin go beyond the available evidence; good sleep is the stated goal, and the curtain is one means to it. Retailer claims about performance have not been independently verified.

lead: Blackout curtains are window coverings made from, or lined with, an opaque fabric that blocks most outside light from entering a room. The term blackout refers to a foam-backed opaque fabric most often seen as hotel curtain lining or drapery [1]. They are popular with people who sleep during the day, with parents of infants, and with residents of areas with heavy night-time light pollution [1].

In looksmaxxing and sleep-optimisation circles they are treated as a basic bedroom measure for darker, more consistent sleep, on the reasoning that adequate sleep supports skin, mood and hormone regulation. Beyond light control, blackout fabrics are also said to provide some thermal insulation and noise dampening because of their density [1].

Evidence specific to curtains is limited. Surveys show that they are among the most common light-reduction measures adults adopt [2], and observational studies link outdoor artificial light at night with metabolic disease [3]. However, a representative Norwegian survey found no association between blackout-curtain use and chronic insomnia disorder [4], and no published trial in the sources reviewed here tests curtains directly against an uncovered window.
infobox: Ordinary household textile; not a medical device

paras: Blackout fabric is made by coating a base textile with layers of foam, each layer being called a pass. In a 2-pass blackout, a black foam layer is applied first and a white or light-coloured layer is applied over it. In a 3-pass blackout, a white layer goes on first, then black foam, then a final white or light layer [1]. The process is credited to Baltimore-based Rockland Industries [1].

Because the black foam layer shows through the fabric side of a 2-pass material, a 2-pass blackout is not generally used as a decorative fabric by itself. A 3-pass material can serve as decorative fabric and blackout lining in a single piece [1]. Blackout is also used for wallpaper, projector screens and planetarium domes [1].

Curtains in general come in many heading styles, lengths and fabrics, and the Grokipedia entry on curtains lists blackout curtains among the common types alongside sheer, pleated, grommet-top and café styles [5]. Edge gaps around a curtain can still let light in, so fit, overlap and rod placement affect how dark the room becomes.

Curtains as a category are old, with the Grokipedia curtains article tracing hangings of linen and other materials to ancient Egypt and later to European castles and Renaissance interiors [5]. That article is AI-generated and its history is not independently verified here. The foam-coated blackout process is a modern industrial development attributed to Rockland Industries [1].

Light reaching the eyes during sleep can arouse the sleeper, and light at night is associated with suppressed melatonin and a weakened signal that it is night. A blackout curtain aims to lower the amount of street, vehicle or early-morning light entering the room. Wikipedia notes use by shift workers sleeping in daylight and in nurseries where darkness is said to help babies sleep [1].
No randomized trial of blackout curtains for sleep or appearance outcomes appears in the sources reviewed here. The available human data are surveys and observational studies.

A 2017 population-based Norwegian telephone survey of 1,001 adults described age and sex differences in bedroom habits and preferences, including whether bedroom windows were left open [6]. A follow-up analysis of the same sample compared people with chronic insomnia disorder with good sleepers. Insomnia was associated with worse bed comfort, more noise, and higher summer bedroom temperature, but the authors found no association with the use of blackout curtains, among other characteristics [4]. The design is cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether curtains change sleep.

A 2025 nationwide cross-sectional survey of 5,006 Polish adults aged 18 to 64 found blackout curtains to be the most common individual measure for reducing night-time light, used by 41.4 percent of respondents, ahead of limiting evening screen time (17.6 percent); eye masks were the least common at 3.9 percent, and 65 percent had adopted at least one such measure [2].

A hospital-admissions study in Ningxia, China, estimated that about 26.8 percent of metabolic-disease cases were attributable to outdoor artificial light at night, with men aged 46 to 59 appearing more susceptible; the authors proposed measures such as universal access to indoor blackout curtains [3]. This is an ecological estimate of outdoor light exposure and does not test curtains.

A survey of nurses on shift work listed blackout curtains among interventions respondents were interested in, alongside an on-site exercise facility, nutrition consulting and block scheduling [7]. It measured interest rather than outcomes.

Blackout curtains are ordinary household textiles and no specific adverse effects are documented in the sources reviewed. Practical considerations noted in consumer guidance include light leaking around the edges and reduced morning daylight, which some people find makes waking harder. Some users pair curtains with a sunrise alarm or open them on waking; these are practices rather than studied recommendations.

In sleep-focused looksmaxxing, darkness is often presented as the first step toward deeper sleep, on the theory that sleep quality influences skin condition and hormones. Curtains are commonly grouped with sleep masks, white noise machines, cooler bedroom temperatures and consistent wake times. The inference from sleep quality to appearance is indirect, and the sources reviewed do not test curtains against appearance outcomes.

Product descriptions typically distinguish between 2-pass and 3-pass construction, full blackout versus partial room-darkening fabric, thermal lining, and heading types that affect how closely the panel seals against the wall [1]. Prices commonly fall between about $25 and $80 per panel set. Manufacturers' light-blocking percentages are retailer claims rather than independent measurements.
